chunks.text: Princess Savitri set out on a long journey to find a husband, visiting many holy places, and came home to her father's palace, where the wise sage Narada was visiting. Her father asked her to say who she had chosen.

Savitri told them about a kind prince named Satyavan. His father, King Dyumatsena, had lost his eyesight and then lost his kingdom, so the family lived quietly in the forest. Satyavan had grown up there, and Savitri had chosen him in her heart.

But Narada said something sad: Satyavan was brave, wise, and good — but he had only one year left to live. Savitri's father begged her to choose someone else, but Savitri said a person can only choose a husband once, and she would not change her mind. Narada agreed that she should marry Satyavan, and then rose into the sky and went back to heaven.

Savitri's father took her to the forest, and King Dyumatsena welcomed her as his son's bride. Savitri gave up her fine clothes for simple ones and lived happily with Satyavan's family, working hard and speaking kindly to everyone — but she never forgot what Narada had said.

As the day Narada spoke of came near, Savitri stopped eating for three days and nights, keeping a careful vow. When the day came, Satyavan picked up his axe to gather wood in the forest, and Savitri asked to go with him. His parents said yes.

While Satyavan was cutting wood, his head began to hurt, and he lay down with his head on Savitri's lap to rest. Then Savitri saw someone frightening standing near them — a shining figure dressed in red, holding a rope. It was Yama, the god of death, and he told her that Satyavan's time had come.

Yama gently pulled Satyavan's life out of his body and began walking away with it. Savitri got up and followed him, even though he told her to go back. She spoke to Yama with such wisdom and courage that he was pleased with her, and he offered her a gift — any gift except her husband's life.

Savitri asked for her father-in-law's eyesight back — he granted it. She kept following and asked for his kingdom back — granted. She asked for a hundred sons for her own father — granted. Then she asked for a hundred sons for herself, with Satyavan as their father — granted too! But then Savitri said this last gift could not come true without her husband alive, so she asked for one more thing: give me back Satyavan's life.

With a cheerful heart, Yama said, "So be it." He untied the rope and gave Satyavan back his life, promising the couple four hundred happy years together. Savitri hurried back to her husband, and he woke up as if from a long sleep.

Back at the hermitage, Dyumatsena had suddenly gotten his eyesight back and had been searching worriedly for his son all night. When Savitri and Satyavan finally arrived, everyone was overjoyed, and Savitri told them the whole wonderful story.

The next day, messengers came with more good news: the enemy who had taken Dyumatsena's kingdom had been defeated, and the people wanted their true king back. Dyumatsena returned to his throne, Satyavan ruled beside him, and in time Savitri had a hundred sons of her own. Because of her love and her clever words, Savitri saved her husband and brought good fortune to both families.
